title: Junior Associate
source: Exercises and worked solutions from "Economies, Accounts and Money" (Integrated Edition), rewritten as customer questions.

questions.text: Calculus refresher for my MBA prep course. Can you differentiate these? (a) 3x⁴ − 2x + 7; (b) ln(x² + 1); (c) x·e^(−2x); (d) (2x + 1)/(x − 3); (e) 100 × 1.04^t with respect to t.
Our cost function is C(q) = {F} + {a}q + {b}q². What's marginal cost at q = {q}, and what's the exact cost of producing unit number {=q+1}? Why are they different?
questions.solution: C′(q) = {a} + {=2*b}q, so C′({q}) = {mc:2}. Exact cost of unit {=q+1}: C({=q+1}) − C({q}) = {disc:2}. The derivative is a local slope; because C is convex (marginal cost rises), the discrete cost exceeds C′({q}) by ½C″ × 1² = {b}.

questions.text: On x > 0, is each of these concave, convex or neither? (a) √x; (b) x² − 4x; (c) ln x; (d) x³ − 3x.
questions.solution: (a) f″ = −¼x^(−3/2) < 0: concave. (b) f″ = 2: convex. (c) f″ = −1/x²: concave. (d) f″ = 6x > 0 for x > 0: convex on x > 0 (but not on the whole real line).

questions.text: Without a calculator: use a first-order and a second-order approximation of f(x) = √x around x = 1 to estimate √1.1. How close do you get to the true value?
questions.solution: f(1) = 1, f′(1) = ½, f″(1) = −¼. First order: 1 + 0.5 × 0.1 = 1.05. Second order: 1.05 − ⅛ × 0.01 = 1.04875. True value: 1.048809 — the second-order term removes most of the error.

questions.text: Demand for our product is Q = {a} − {b}P. What's the price elasticity at P = {P}? At what price is demand unit-elastic, and what's revenue there?
questions.solution: At P = {P}, Q = {=a-b*P} and ε = −{b} × {P}/{=a-b*P} = {=-b*P/(a-b*P):3}. Unit elasticity: {b}P/({a} − {b}P) = 1 → P = {=a/(2*b):2}, Q = {=a/2}, revenue = {=a*a/(4*b):2} — the maximum revenue. For linear demand, unit elasticity is always at the midpoint of the curve.

questions.topic: Profit maximisation with a capacity limit
questions.text: We sell at a fixed market price of ${p}. Our cost is C(q) = {F} + {a}q + 0.5q². What output maximises profit, and what's the profit? Can you verify it's a maximum? And what if our capacity is only {cap} units?
questions.solution: Π = {p}q − {F} − {a}q − 0.5q². FOC: {=p-a} − q = 0 → q* = {=p-a} (price = marginal cost {a} + q). Π = {=(p-a)^2/2-F:2}. Π″ = −1 < 0, so it's a maximum. With capacity {cap} < {=p-a}, Π′ > 0 on [0, {cap}], so produce q = {cap}: Π = {=p*cap-F-a*cap-0.5*cap^2:2}.

questions.text: Can you show me two iterations of Newton's method on f(x) = x² − {k}, starting from x₀ = {x0}? What number is it approximating?
questions.solution: x₁ = x₀ − f(x₀)/f′(x₀) = {x0} − ({=x0^2-k})/{=2*x0} = {x1:5}; x₂ = x₁ − (x₁² − {k})/(2x₁) = {x2:5}. It approximates √{k} = {=sqrt(k):5}.

questions.text: My utility function is U(x, y) = x^{a}·y^{=1-a:1}. What are Uₓ and U_y, and what's the slope of the indifference curve through ({x}, {y})?
Show that F(K, L) = 2K^0.5·L^0.5 is homogeneous of degree one, and verify Euler's theorem at K = 16, L = 4.
Find and classify the critical point of f(x, y) = 10x + 8y − x² + xy − y².
questions.solution: fₓ = 10 − 2x + y = 0 and f_y = 8 + x − 2y = 0. From the first, y = 2x − 10; then 8 + x − 4x + 20 = 0 → x = 28/3, y = 26/3. f_xx = −2, f_yy = −2, f_xy = 1: det H = 4 − 1 = 3 > 0 with f_xx < 0, so it is a (global) maximum.

questions.text: Simple Laffer model: tax revenue is R(τ) = τ·B₀(1 − τ)^e, so the tax base shrinks as the rate rises. If e = {e}, what's the revenue-maximising tax rate? If the actual rate is {t}%, would a small rise in the rate raise or lower revenue?
questions.solution: R′(τ) has the sign of (1 − τ) − eτ, so τ* = 1/(1 + e) = {=100/(1+e):1}%. At τ = {t}%: (1 − {=t/100:2}) − {e} × {=t/100:2} = {=(1-t/100)-e*t/100:3}, which is {?(1-t/100)-e*t/100>0|positive, so a small rise would raise revenue|negative, so a small rise would lower revenue}.

questions.text: Maximise U = x^(1/3)·y^(2/3) subject to x + 2y = {m}. What are x*, y* and λ*, and can you verify that λ* equals the derivative of maximum utility with respect to income?
questions.solution: Tangency: MUₓ/MU_y = y/(2x) = 1/2 → y = x. Then 3x = {m}, so x* = y* = {=m/3}: one-third of income is spent on x and two-thirds on y, matching the exponents. λ* = MUₓ/pₓ = (1/3)(y/x)^(2/3) = 1/3. With income m, x = y = m/3, so V(m) = m/3 and V′(m) = 1/3 = λ*.

questions.text: I have {F} metres of fencing to enclose a rectangular field along a straight river (no fence needed on the river side). What dimensions maximise the area, and what's the shadow value of an extra metre of fencing?
questions.solution: With two sides x perpendicular to the river and one side y parallel: maximise xy subject to 2x + y = {F}. A = x({F} − 2x) is maximised at x = {=F/4}, y = {=F/2}, area {=F^2/8}. With fencing F, A = F²/8, so A′(F) = F/4 = {=F/4} square metres per extra metre — the Lagrange multiplier (λ = x = {=F/4}).

questions.text: A consumer has U = x^0.5·y^0.5, income 100, and prices pₓ = 2 and p_y = 4 (so x* = 25 and λ* ≈ 0.1768). Use the envelope theorem to find the effect on maximum utility of a small rise in pₓ, and check it by writing maximum utility V as a function of pₓ.

Our production function is q = K^0.5·L^0.5. The wage is w = {w} and the rental rate of capital is r = {r}. What input mix minimises the cost of producing q = {q}? What's the minimum cost and the marginal cost?
questions.solution: Tangency: K/L = w/r = {w}/{r}, so K = {=w/r:3}L. Then q = √(K·L) = L√({=w/r:3}) = {q} → L = {=q/sqrt(w/r):3}, K = {=q*sqrt(w/r):3}. Cost = wL + rK = {cost:2}. In general C(q) = 2q√(wr) = {=2*sqrt(w*r):2}q, so marginal cost = average cost = {=2*sqrt(w*r):2} (constant returns to scale).

questions.text: A consumer has U = 2√x + y, income 10, and p_y = 1. What's the optimal bundle when pₓ = 0.5, and when pₓ = 0.05? What happens if income were only 5 with pₓ = 0.05?
questions.solution: Interior condition MUₓ/pₓ = MU_y/p_y: x^(−1/2)/pₓ = 1, so x = 1/pₓ². At pₓ = 0.5: x = 4 (spending 2), y = 8. At pₓ = 0.05: x = 400 would cost 20, more than income, so it's a corner: y = 0, x = 10/0.05 = 200. With income 5 the corner is x = 100, y = 0: the non-negativity constraint on y binds.

questions.text: A household has utility ln c₁ + ln c₂, earns {y1} now and {y2} next period, the interest rate is {r}%, and it cannot borrow. What will it consume in each period? And what would it consume if it could borrow freely?
questions.solution: Wealth W = {y1} + {y2}/{=1+r/100:2} = {W:2}. Unconstrained c₁ = W/2 = {=W/2:2} > {y1}, so the borrowing constraint binds: c₁ = {y1}, c₂ = {y2} (with a positive multiplier on the constraint). With free borrowing: c₁ = {=W/2:2}, c₂ = {=W/2*(1+r/100):2}.

questions.text: Maximise 3x + 2y subject to x + y ≤ 8, x + 3y ≤ 12, x ≤ 5, x, y ≥ 0. What's the optimal corner, and what are the shadow prices of the three constraints?
questions.solution: Corners: (0,0), (5,0), (5, 7/3), (0,4); x + y ≤ 8 never binds. Values: 0, 15, 15 + 14/3 = 19.67, 8. Optimum (5, 7/3), value 59/3 ≈ 19.67. Shadow prices: x + y ≤ 8 is slack → 0. For the binding constraints, y₂ + y₃ = 3 and 3y₂ = 2 give y₂ = 2/3 (for x + 3y ≤ 12) and y₃ = 7/3 (for x ≤ 5). Check: 12 × 2/3 + 5 × 7/3 = 59/3.

questions.text: Our factory makes A and B. Machine time: 2A + B ≤ 120 hours; labour: A + 3B ≤ 150 hours. Profit per unit was 40 for A and 50 for B, but B's contribution has just risen to 90. What's the new optimal plan, what are the shadow prices of machine time and labour, and which resource became more valuable?
questions.solution: Corners: (60,0) → 2,400; (0,50) → 4,500; (42,36) → 1,680 + 3,240 = 4,920. Still (42, 36). Dual: 2y₁ + y₂ = 40, y₁ + 3y₂ = 90 → y₁ = 6 (machine hour), y₂ = 28 (labour hour); check 720 + 4,200 = 4,920. Labour, used intensively by the now more profitable product B, has become more valuable; machine time less so.

questions.text: In a model of our bank's profit maximisation, the multiplier on the regulator's minimum capital ratio is 0.04 per unit of capital. What does that number mean, and why isn't it just our cost of issuing shares?
questions.solution: It's the rate at which maximum profit would rise if the requirement were relaxed so one less unit of capital were needed — the marginal cost of the regulation to the bank's objective, inside the model. It isn't the cost of issuing shares (a market transaction cost): the shadow price reflects everything that makes capital constraining (e.g. forgone profitable lending), and it is local — a large relaxation wouldn't be worth 0.04 per unit throughout.

questions.text: Can you find these integrals? (a) ∫(6x² − 4x + 3) dx; (b) ∫e^(−0.05t) dt; (c) ∫(2/x) dx; (d) ∫x·e^(2x) dx.
questions.solution: (a) 2x³ − 2x² + 3x + C. (b) −20e^(−0.05t) + C. (c) 2 ln|x| + C. (d) By parts (u = x, dv = e^(2x) dx): ½x·e^(2x) − ¼e^(2x) + C.

questions.text: Evaluate: (a) ∫₀³ 2q dq; (b) ∫₁⁴ x^(−1/2) dx; (c) ∫₀¹⁰ e^(−0.1t) dt.
Our marginal cost is MC(q) = {a} + {b}q and fixed cost is {F}. What's total cost at q = {q1}, and what does it cost to increase output from {q1} to {q2}?
Inverse demand is P = {a} − {b}Q and inverse supply is P = {c} + {d}Q. What's the equilibrium, consumer surplus and producer surplus?

A central bank buys bonds at a rate that rises steadily from 0 to {k} billion a month over a year: b(t) = {=k/12:2}t billion per month for t between 0 and 12 months. By how much does its bond holding rise over the year?
questions.solution: Integrate the flow: ∫₀¹² {=k/12:2}t dt = {=k/12:2} × 144/2 = {=k*6} billion.

questions.text: A licence produces income of €{c} a year continuously for {n} years. What's its present value at a continuously compounded rate of {r}%? What would a perpetual licence be worth? And one whose income grows at {g}% a year forever?
A density is f(x) = 2x on [0, 1] and zero elsewhere. Can you check it integrates to one, and find P(X ≤ {a}) and P(X > {b})?

questions.topic: Gini coefficient from a Lorenz curve
questions.text: What's the Gini coefficient for the Lorenz curve L(p) = 0.4p + 0.6p²? Is that society more or less equal than one with L(p) = p²?
questions.solution: ∫₀¹ (0.4p + 0.6p²) dp = 0.2 + 0.2 = 0.4, so G = 1 − 2 × 0.4 = 0.2. For L = p², ∫ = 1/3 and G = 1/3, so the first society is more equal.

questions.text: (a) Solve ẋ = −0.2(x − 50) with x(0) = 10. What's x(5), and what's the half-life? (b) In a logistic adoption model with k = 0.8 and saturation level 100, starting from x₀ = 2, when does adoption reach 50? And 90?
Use Euler's method with steps of 0.5 to approximate x(1) for ẋ = {k}x with x(0) = {x0}. Compare with the exact value and with a single step of 1.
questions.solution: Steps of 0.5: {x0} × (1 + {=k/2})² = {=x0*(1+k/2)^2:2}. Exact: {x0}e^{k} = {=x0*exp(k):2}. One step of 1: {x0} × {=1+k} = {=x0*(1+k):2}. Halving the step roughly halves the error ({=x0*exp(k)-x0*(1+k):2} vs {=x0*exp(k)-x0*(1+k/2)^2:2}).

questions.topic: Dot products and a price index
questions.text: A household buys the bundle q = ({q1}, {q2}, {q3}) at prices p = ({p1}, {p2}, {p3}). What does it spend? Next year prices are ({n1}, {n2}, {n3}). What does the same bundle cost, and what's the percentage change?
questions.solution: p·q = {=p1*q1} + {=p2*q2} + {=p3*q3} = {s0}. New cost = {=n1*q1:2} + {=n2*q2:2} + {=n3*q3:2} = {s1:2}: a change of {=(s1/s0-1)*100:2}% — a fixed-basket price index.

questions.text: Let A = [[1, 2], [0, 3]] and B = [[4, 0], [1, 2]] (rows listed). Compute AB, BA and (AB)′, and verify that (AB)′ = B′A′.
Solve: 2x + y − z = 3, x − y + 2z = 7, 3x + 2y + z = 10.
questions.solution: From the second, x = 7 + y − 2z. Substituting: 3y − 5z = −11 and 5y − 5z = −11. Subtracting gives 2y = 0, so y = 0, z = 11/5 = 2.2, x = 7 − 4.4 = 2.6. Check: 5.2 + 0 − 2.2 = 3 ✓.

questions.text: Find the inverse of [[4, 3], [2, 2]] and use it to solve 4x + 3y = 18, 2x + 2y = 10.
For which value of k is the matrix [[2, k], [3, 6]] singular? For that k, does the system 2x + ky = 4, 3x + 6y = 6 have no solution or infinitely many?
questions.solution: det = 12 − 3k = 0 at k = 4. Then 2x + 4y = 4 is x + 2y = 2 and 3x + 6y = 6 is also x + 2y = 2: the same line, so infinitely many solutions.

questions.text: Two related goods. Market 1 clears when 5p₁ − p₂ = 85. In market 2, demand is Q₂ = 60 + p₁ − 3p₂ and supply used to be Q₂ = 5 + 2p₂, which gave p₁ = 20, p₂ = 15. Supply of good 2 has fallen to Q₂ = −7 + 2p₂. Using Cramer's rule, what are the new prices, and why does the price of good 1 change too?
questions.solution: Market 2 now clears when 60 + p₁ − 3p₂ = −7 + 2p₂, i.e. −p₁ + 5p₂ = 67 (up from 55). det = 25 − 1 = 24. p₁ = (85 × 5 + 67)/24 = 20.5; p₂ = (5 × 67 + 85)/24 = 17.5. Good 2's price rises 2.5; buyers switch toward the substitute good 1, raising its price by 0.5.

questions.text: Two industries: one unit of manufactures uses 0.2 manufactures and 0.4 services; one unit of services uses 0.3 manufactures and 0.1 services. If final demand for services rises by {d}, by how much must each industry's gross output rise? Why does manufacturing output rise even though final demand for manufactures didn't change?
questions.solution: (I − A) = [[0.8, −0.3], [−0.4, 0.9]], det = 0.60, (I − A)⁻¹ = [[1.5, 0.5], [0.667, 1.333]]. Δx = (I − A)⁻¹(0, {d})′ = ({=0.5*d:1}, {=4/3*d:1}). Services use manufactured inputs (0.3 per unit), and those manufactures need services and manufactures in turn — the indirect requirements raise manufacturing output.

questions.text: Classify each symmetric matrix as positive definite, negative (semi)definite or indefinite: [[2, 1], [1, 3]], [[−4, 2], [2, −1]] and [[1, 3], [3, 1]].
questions.solution: First: a₁₁ = 2 > 0, det = 5 > 0 → positive definite. Second: a₁₁ = −4 < 0, det = 4 − 4 = 0 → negative semidefinite (not definite). Third: det = 1 − 9 = −8 < 0 → indefinite.

questions.text: What are the eigenvalues of A = [[0.9, 0.3], [0.2, 0.4]]? Is the system x(t+1) = A·x(t) stable?
questions.solution: Trace 1.3, determinant 0.36 − 0.06 = 0.30: λ = (1.3 ± √(1.69 − 1.2))/2 = (1.3 ± 0.7)/2 = 1.0 or 0.3. One eigenvalue equals 1, so the system is not stable in the strict sense: deviations along that eigenvector persist forever (a unit root).

questions.text: Each year {s}% of investment-grade firms keep their rating and the rest are downgraded to speculative grade; {u}% of speculative-grade firms are upgraded and the rest stay. What's the long-run (stationary) distribution? If all firms start investment grade, what share is speculative grade after two years?
